title: Inquest calls for greater police aid
article: A coroner's jury says overall safety would be enhanced if two police officers transported mentally distraught people to hospital.

The four-man jury examining the death of Mladen Cujko also recommended staffing levels of RCMP detachments be reviewed to establish a minimum standard -- a process already being studied at the national level.
"We're examining a model by which we can determine adequate staffing levels for detachments," Island District RCMP Supt. Jim Good said Tuesday. "A national study is being done now."
The inquest into the death of Cujko, a 33-year-old known drug user from Burnaby, wrapped up Friday. The inquest was mandatory because Cujko died in police custody.

Forensic pathologist Dr. Laurel Gray testified that Cujko died of a cardiac arrest brought on by five times the minimum lethal limit of cocaine in his body. There was also evidence that he had smoked crack cocaine.
West Shore RCMP picked up Cujko at 9:18 p.m. on Aug. 21 after callers reported that a distraught man was running in and out of traffic at the intersection of Jacklin Road and Goldstream Avenue.

Cujko was arrested under Section 28 of the Mental Health Act and was very calm and co-operative when he was placed in the back of the RCMP car. Const. Murray Bayles started driving him to the Royal Jubilee Hospital for a psychiatric assessment.
Evidence was presented at the inquest that Cujko became agitated and started trying to kick out the rear window.

"Const. Bayles was north of the Six Mile exit, driving into Victoria," said coroner's counsel Kenn Kardish. "He knew he had a long way to go to reach the Jubilee and he was concerned Mr. Cujko might escape the police vehicle."
Bayles stopped the car and opened the rear door on the driver's side, said Kardish. He tried to subdue Cujko with pepper spray, but it had no effect. Cujko fought his way out of the police car.

Bayles applied a lateral restraint hold, an approved hold that briefly cuts off the blood supply to the brain by suppressing the carotid arteries on either side of the neck. A lateral restraint hold is different from a chokehold, where the forearm is placed directly against a person's throat.
Cujko blacked out, and Bayles tried to handcuff him behind his back. One of cuffs became locked in the other, so Bayles was unable to put the handcuffs on both wrists, said Kardish.

Within seconds, Cujko had regained consciousness and was kicking and struggling again. At that point, two off-duty paramedics heading north on the highway towards Nanaimo saw what was happening and stopped to offer help. One of the paramedics ran across the highway and helped Bayles hold down Cujko.
Const. Tracy Horwood arrived and helped Bayles get the handcuffs on Cujko. They rolled Cujko on to his back and noticed he wasn't breathing, said Kardish. The paramedic began CPR without success.
Kardish said he was satisfied the jury had made appropriate recommendations.
"The jury felt it would have been better if two officers had been present," he said.
The jury also recommended that protective equipment, similar to the caging on the side windows of the police car, be installed on the rear window of police cars.
